Title: F5 releases emergency patches for critical BIG-IP RCE flaws
Context: Most recently, in September, F5 also patched a critical BIG-IP APM vulnerability (CVE-2026-94127) that is being actively exploited in zero-day remote code execution attacks
Full Text:
US cybersecurity company F5 warned customers to patch five BIG-IP vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to trigger denial-of-service (DoS) or gain remote code execution.

Tracked as CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-116953, and CVE-2026-123637, these stack-based buffer overflow flaws affect the company's BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) centralized access management proxy solution and the BIG-IP iRules programmable scripting feature.

All five security issues are rated critical severity, and unauthenticated threat actors can exploit them to terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute arbitrary code remotely on systems with vulnerable configurations.

The company also released engineering hotfixes for a high-severity BIG-IP APM SAML vulnerability (CVE-2026-126822) stemming from an integer underflow (wrap or wraparound) weakness that remote, unauthenticated threat actors can abuse in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

"Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system and may perform RCE," F5 said. "There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only."

F5 said it has no mitigation measures for these flaws and advised security teams to install the out-of-band hotfixes released on Wednesday to address them on vulnerable devices.

Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver currently tracks more than 177,000 BIG-IP instances and over 14,600 IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints exposed online. However, there is no information on how many are honeypots or have already been patched against these vulnerabilities.

Although the company hasn't flagged any of these issues as exploited in attacks, admins should upgrade systems to the latest version as soon as possible, since cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often abused F5 vulnerabilities in the wild.

Attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive files from victims worldwide in recent years.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged seven F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited since November 2021, four of them also used by ransomware gangs.

Most recently, in September, F5 also patched a critical BIG-IP APM vulnerability (CVE-2026-94127) that is being actively exploited in zero-day remote code execution attacks.

One year ago, F5 also disclosed that state-backed hackers breached its systems in August 2025 to steal source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities.

F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to more than 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 of Fortune 50 companies.

Title: NGINX2Root: F5 patches five critical NGINX vulnerabilities
Context: A public proof-of-concept exploit for one of them (CVE-2026-123007) is already available, though
Full Text:
F5 has patched five critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the world’s most widely used open-source web server, that can allow remote code execution under certain conditions.

Dubbed “NGINX2Root” by Xint researchers, two of the bunch (CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007) were also independently unearthed and reported by Rapid7, Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Palo Alto Networks and Metnir researchers.

There’s no evidence that any of them has been exploited in the wild, and none were on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog as of November 19. A public proof-of-concept exploit for one of them (CVE-2026-123007) is already available, though.

The NGINX2Root vulnerabilities

NGINX is a web server, but it’s also used as a reverse proxy, load balancer, mail proxy, static file server, and HTTP cache.

The NGINX2Root vulnerabilities are:

CVE-2026-123007 (aka “NGINX2Shell”): an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow control, leading to out-of-bounds read/write on the heap, which may lead to a crash of the NGINX worker process and pontentially allow remote code execution.

CVE-2026-123633: a use-after-free that is reachable when HTTP/2 is used and requests are forwarded to an upstream server.

CVE-2026-123634: a use-after-free in NGINX’s DNS resolver. It can only be triggered (via a specially crafted HTTP request) if the server uses the resolver, request-derived proxy_pass, and mirror (with mirror_request_body off) directives together.

CVE-2026-121810: a use-after-free from closing a QUIC connection while an HTTP/3 request runs

CVE-2026-113425: a use-after-free in the mail proxy’s auth_http path

If address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, any of the five can allow remote code execution with the privileges of the NGINX worker process.

To get from there to root, attackers need a sixth flaw, and Xint found that one too: a use-after-free in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code that can turn into a double free. The researchers used it to get root on cloud hosts, and also got a root shell on the host from a Docker container. (The Linux kernel flaw has no CVE as of November 18 and hasn’t been patched yet).

Xint and Wiz have built proof-of-concept exploits for the five flaws, but haven’t released them yet.

Rapid7’s Stephen Fewer has published a technical analysis and a PoC exploit for CVE-2026-123007.

“Rapid7 describes the exploit as constrained: it depends on a glibc memory-copy routine specific to x86-64 builds, requires roughly 128 gigabytes of HTTP/2 traffic, and needs to defeat ASLR by recovering heap addresses from server responses. Execution lands in the NGINX worker process,” Tenable researchers noted.

“The exploit is also unlikely to succeed against servers behind HTTP/2-terminating proxies or on connections too slow to deliver the required data volume before NGINX’s one-hour connection limit is reached,” they added

What to do?

Mitigations are available, but upgrading to a fixed release – NGINX Open Source versions 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, NGINX Plus versions 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 – is the better option. (F5 also fixed five more NGINX flaws in the same releases.)

Admins should upgrade and then restart NGINX, because a configuration reload doesn’t replace the running executable. Those who use distro packages should check for backported fixes.

NGINX is also part of other F5 products, such as NGINX Instance Manager, NGINX Ingress Controller and NGINX Gateway Fabric. F5 has released updates for some of them and is still working on the rest.

Xint researchers also provided instructions on how to investigate possible attacks via CVE-2026-123007.

Johannes Ullrich, dean of research at the SANS Technology Institute, says that large organizations probably won’t manage to patch all their NGINX instances before exploits appear, so they should think beyond these vulnerabilities.

His general advice to meet the ongoing “vulnocalypse” is to automate patching as much as possible, cut the number of internet-facing systems, and limit which data and resources each application can access.

Title: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
Context: Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts
Full Text:
Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts.

Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent.

F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround.

The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company.

None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself.

Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition.

Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server:

CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only.

CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.

CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.

CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.

CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.

CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected.

F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX.

For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed.

The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work.

A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team.

BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285.

The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe.

Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.

That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings.

Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws

Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1:

CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups.

CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed.

CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws.

CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks.

CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact.

CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.
